newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end lower as rate worries persist.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end lower as rate worries persist.

text.p: The prices of U.S. government securities ended lower Monday after a session marked by little economic news and much speculation.

The only economic news traders saw was a stronger housing index from the National Association of Home Builders, another indication of strength in that critical sector. They also had market-negative comments from Federal Reserve officials to mull over and yields on the the long bond 7.0 percent for the first time since the September 23 close last year. The 30-year Treasury bond closed down 5/32 at 95-27/32 to yield 6.96 percent.

San Francisco Fed president Robert Parry, in a speech delivered in Germany, said he saw few signs of wage pressures in U.S. labor markets. Earlier, a news wire reported that Fed governor Edward Kelley said that as wage-price pressures continued to rise the real federal funds rate was not restrictive but neutral.

Bond market participants doubted there would be any significant movement during the week before the Fed's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee meeting on March 25. Rather, they said, nervousness about a potential tightening would cast a negative pall on the market all week.

Christopher Iggo, economist at BZW Securities Inc., said comments from Kelley and Parry were market negative. He said a comeback seen during the afternoon after yields on the long bond reached 7.0 percent were most likely just an indication of an oversold market.
Iggo said the bounce was probably enough to get people to return to looking at technical charts. He doubted many investors would go into next week's FOMC meeting holding aggressively long positions.
Increasingly, investors were harried at the prospect of the Fed tightening next week, he said.
Michelle Laughlin, economist at Prudential Securities Inc., said the improvement seen in midafternoon was strictly a matter of traders covering short positions.
"We have the continued expectation we'll see a rate hike of 25 basis points on March 25. (Rates) could be hiked as much as another 50 basis points by midsummer," Laughlin said.

"People are just starting to get a better sense of things. They reflected over the weekend on last week's strong retail sales report, and while it's very uncertain, people are resigned to tightening," said Mark Vitner, capital markets economist at First Union Corp.
Vitner said the real question was how many times the Fed would have to tighten in order to slow the economy as its protracted recovery continued.
"In the past the market would sell off severely after an initial tightening. But this time we're not looking at that scenario as people see the good news on inflation," Vitner said.
He thought the Fed would only have to move twice over the coming months before returning to a neutral bias. Vitner said there was a 50-50 chance of a tightening on March 25.
The next data the market will see is February housing starts, expected to be strong, on Tuesday at 830 EST/1330 GMT.
The Treasury's auction of three- and six-month bills yielded an average of 5.13 and 5.26 percent, respectively.

At the short end of the maturity range, three-month bills closed up two basis points at 5.12 percent; six-month bills were up four basis points at 5.24 percent and year-bill rates ended up three basis points at 5.45 percent.
Two-year notes were down 2/32 at 99-13/32, yielding 6.20 percent. Five-year notes were down 4/32 to 98-24/32, yielding 6.55 percent. Ten-year notes fell 5/32 to 96-21/32, yielding 6.72 percent.
